extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and patent judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for assessing inventive step (non-obviousness) of patent claims, drawing on JPO, EPO and USPTO examination guidelines and related proposals. Covers selection of prior art, problem-and-solution/could-would reasoning, positive/negative factors and evidentiary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of primary prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner selects the prior art most suitable for the reasoning (hereinafter referred to as 'the primary prior art'). The examiner should not regard the combination of two or more independent pieces of prior art as the primary prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a single reference that is the most promising starting point for development to the invention; do not treat a mere aggregation of multiple references as the primary prior art. This selection affects what combinations are plausible and whether obstructive factors exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine inventive step for each claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are two or more claims, the examiner should determine the existence of an inventive step for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inventive step claim-by-claim rather than treating a multi-claim application as a single unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step inventive-step reasoning (JPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner determines whether it is possible to reason that a skilled person would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by following steps (1)–(4): (1) determine possibility based on factors supporting non-existence (using secondary prior art or common general knowledge); (2) if impossible then inventive step exists; (3) if possible, comprehensively assess factors supporting existence; (4) if impossible then inventive step exists; if still possible, no inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the sequence precisely: first attempt to show lack of inventive step using motivating factors; if that succeeds, then check whether positive/obstructive factors change the conclusion. The process is iterative and requires weighing both sets of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for applying secondary prior art to primary prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If combining secondary prior art (B) with primary prior art (A) yields the claimed invention, the motivation to attempt that combination is a factor supporting non-existence of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine motivation by comprehensively considering the following points of view: (1) relation of technical fields, (2) similarity of problems to be solved, (3) similarity of operations or functions, (4) suggestions shown in the content of prior art. It is not sufficient to rely on only one point of view; consider them together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of technical fields (motivation subfactor)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ordinary creativity for a skilled person to apply technical means from related technical fields to solve problems in the primary prior art. Presence of related technical means in related fields can be grounds for motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relation of technical fields alongside at least one other motivation viewpoint; if 'technical field' determination already involves problems/operations/products, it may subsume other viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of problems to be solved (motivation subfactor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity between the problems addressed by primary and secondary prior art supports motivation to combine them where those problems would be obvious or easily conceived by the skilled person at the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess similarity based on the state of the art at filing; include cases where the claimed invention's problem isn't recognizable (e.g., trial-and-error inventions) — still consider differing reasoning processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of operations or functions (motivation subfactor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of operations or functions between primary and secondary prior art can justify applying or associating the secondary prior art with the primary prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for analogous functional or operational features that would lead a skilled person to transfer techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions in the content of prior art (motivation subfactor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions shown in the content of prior art for applying the secondary prior art to the primary prior art are strong evidence of motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit teaching, hints, or pointers in prior art that would prompt combination weigh heavily toward obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design variation (factor supporting non-existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a skilled person would arrive at the differing elements by ordinary design variations starting from the primary prior art, this supports non-existence of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (i) selection of optimum materials from publicly known materials, (ii) optimally or preferably modified numerical ranges, (iii) materials replaced by equivalents, (iv) design variation or design choice associated with application of specific techniques. Suggestion in primary prior art for such variations is an effective factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere aggregation of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere aggregation means each claimed element is well-known and their functions/operations are not related to each other; such aggregation is a factor supporting non-existence of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention is simply a juxtaposition of independent known elements with no functional interaction or synergy, it lacks inventive step. Also consider implications of aggregation present within the primary prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects (factor supporting existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantageous effects over the prior art (particular effects given by the claimed invention that are advantageous over prior art) are factors supporting the existence of an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should take into account effects understood from description, claims and drawings. Identify effects that are attributable to distinguishing features and that impart an advantage over cited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstructive factors (factors supporting existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that obstruct application of secondary prior art to primary prior art support existence of an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) secondary prior art applied to primary prior art cannot achieve primary prior art's purpose; (ii) combined prior art cannot adequately function; (iii) secondary prior art is excluded or cannot be adopted by primary prior art; (iv) publications showing the secondary prior art is inferior discourage its application. Also, if a cited prior art's publication contains descriptions that would obstruct a skilled person from arriving at the invention, that prior art may be inappropriate as a citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit considering teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should not omit considering whether there is a factor teaching away from applying well-known art merely because the cited prior art is well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-known references can contain teaching-away material; such indications must be evaluated and can affect inventive-step conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach (EPO) — Stage 1: closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Closest prior art is the single reference disclosing the combination of features constituting the most promising starting point for development leading to the invention; it should be directed to a similar purpose/effect or belong to same/closely related technical field and require minimal structural/functional modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the reference that corresponds to a similar use and requires minimum adaptation; case law (e.g., T 606/89) guides selection. Purpose/effect and technical field are primary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach (EPO) — Stage 2: objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish objectively the technical problem by comparing the application/patent and the closest prior art, identifying distinguishing features and the technical effect produced by them, then formulating the technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features not contributing to technical character cannot support inventive step. The technical problem must not contain pointers to the solution (avoid ex post facto formulation). Effects derivable from the application as filed may be used; new effects submitted later are acceptable only if the skilled person would recognise them as implied or related to the initial technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach (EPO) — Stage 3: could–would (would vs could)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether prior art as a whole would have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify/adapt the closest prior art to arrive at the claimed invention; 'would' (motivating teaching) is required, not just 'could'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ordered questions: (i) Would the skilled person take D2 into account when starting from D1? (consider common general knowledge and incentives), (ii) Could the skilled person find a solution from D2? (level of understanding), (iii) Can the solution from D2 be applied to D1? (technical hurdles, whether more than routine testing is required). If all answers are yes, obviousness is established; a no in any question supports inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs juxtaposition/aggregation (synergy requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed combination of features must be considered as a whole; when features functionally interact to produce a combined technical effect greater than the sum, it's a true combination; if not, it's a mere aggregation and can be shown obvious by showing individual features were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for synergistic functional interaction producing a combined technical effect. If absent, the aggregation rationale suffices for an obviousness finding (EPO case law: T 389/86, T 204/06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition/discovery of a new problem as potential inventive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a problem not previously recognized can itself be a contribution that supports patentability, even if the claimed solution appears non-progressive in retrospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recognition of the problem is an important contribution to the patent achievement, the invention may have inventive step (caveat: introduction of a new problem that merely removes a use deficiency may not confer inventive step).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP examples of obviousness (prima facie case) — combining known elements for predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results supports a prima facie obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection requires: multiple prior arts include each claimed element; a skilled person could have combined them by known methods; a skilled person would have recognized the results as predictable; and separated elements perform the same function.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — simple substitution of known element
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that prior art differs only by substituting one component for another known in the art, that a skilled person could have made that substitution, and the results were predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — using known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods/products) in the same way supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish that the prior art contained a 'base' invention and that the known improvement technique could have been applied by a skilled person in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — applying known technique to a device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show prior art had a base invention containing the known technique and that a skilled person would recognize predictable improved results.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — 'obvious to try' with reasonable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' where selecting from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require: a recognized problem at the time, a finite number of identified predictable solutions, and that a skilled person could have pursued them with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — predictable variations across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field prompting variations for use in same or a different field, if predictable to a skilled person, supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation and whether the variation would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP example — teaching/suggestion/motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led a skilled person to modify or combine references supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that prior art provided a motivation or suggestion that would lead to the claimed combination or modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common procedural elements for inventive-step analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Common steps across jurisdictions: (i) Identification of the claimed invention; (ii) Identification of the primary prior art; (iii) Lifting commonalities and differences between claimed invention and primary prior art; (iv) Analysis of the ease of overcoming such differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by examining whether elements exist in secondary prior art to relieve differences and whether negative or positive elements affect combining primary and secondary prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive and negative elements checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated positive elements (favoring non-inventiveness) and negative elements (favoring inventiveness) to be weighed in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive elements include: close technical-field relevance, similarity of problems/functions, prior-art hints, simple combination, optimizing known materials/numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, workshop modifications, common general application, degenerative inventions, etc. Negative elements include: advantageous effects over cited invention, secondary prior art that contradicts or makes primary prior art nonfunctional when combined, exclusion of application by primary prior art, publication showing inferiority of secondary prior art, commercial success, long-felt unsolved problems, overcoming technical prejudice, failure by others, discovery of new problem or causal mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of particularized allegation for combination (proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject inventive step a petitioner must present reasonable and sufficient logic detailing the process of arriving at the invention from prior art; petitioner should allege a primary prior art and explain in detail how other references combine to produce the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combats hindsight by requiring claimants of obviousness to define the primary prior art and the specific combination path so examiners/courts can evaluate obstructive factors and allow patentees to rebut with factual details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual testing of the skill level of the POSA (proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical skills of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) should be tested by factual inquiry: inventor's education, technical problem, prior-art solutions, innovation rate in field, technical complexity, and education level of skilled practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete factual indicia to ground the POSA construct rather than assuming generic skills; these facts influence whether combinations were routine or required more than ordinary creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of secondary indicia (proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary elements (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) should be proactively analyzed when difficulty of composition and marked effectiveness are unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat secondary indicia as supportive evidence of non-obviousness where appropriate, and relate them to the technical skill level of the POSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cherry-picking and abstract combination (proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing combinations, do not abstract prior art elements beyond the comparison stage nor combine arbitrary extracted elements from multiple references without selecting a primary prior art as a whole; examine prior art references as single inventions and consider conflicts between their full contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from one prior art reference (primary) as a whole and then consider adding whole or partial elements from another (secondary); if combining requires eliminating conflicting elements of the primary reference without justification, such combination is not 'easy' and hindsight should be suspected.
